result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.count_walks()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count walks of a specific length between all pairs of nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19255-L19392){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.count_walks(walk_length) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A walk is a sequence of nodes where each adjacent pair is connected by an edge. Unlike paths, walks can repeat nodes and edges. The number of walks of length `k` from node `i` to node `j` equals the `(i,j)` entry of `A^k` where `A` is the adjacency matrix. This method computes the *k*-th power of the adjacency matrix using fast matrix exponentiation, which is efficient even for large k values. Time complexity: `O(V³ × log k)` where `V` is the number of nodes Space complexity: `O(V²)` ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [walk_length]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Non-negative integer representing the number of edges in the walk. A walk of length `0` means staying at the same node (identity matrix). A walk of length `1` counts direct edges. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, dict[int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Nested dictionary where outer keys are source node IDs, inner keys are target node IDs, and inner values are the number of walks of length `walk_length=` from source to target. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If walk_length is negative. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} **Walk vs. Path**: - a *walk* can repeat nodes and edges (counted by this method) - a *path* cannot repeat nodes (use shortest path algorithms) - a *trail* cannot repeat edges but can repeat nodes **Walk length 0**: Returns the identity matrix where each node has exactly 1 "walk" to itself (staying in place) and 0 walks to other nodes. **Walk length 1**: Returns the adjacency matrix where counts direct edges. For multigraphs, this counts multiple edges between the same node pair. **Growth of walk counts**: The number of walks can grow very quickly, especially in dense graphs and with larger walk lengths. For example, in a complete graph K_n, the number of walks grows exponentially with walk_length. **Applications**: - **Network reachability**: Measure connectivity strength beyond shortest paths - **Information diffusion**: Model how information can spread through multiple redundant paths - **Random walk analysis**: Expected number of random walks between nodes - **Graph similarity**: Compare graphs based on walk structure - **Spectral analysis**: Related to eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix **Relationship to matrix powers**: This method computes `A^k` where `A` is the adjacency matrix. The trace of `A^k` (sum of diagonal elements) counts closed walks (cycles) of length `k`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a 3-node path `0 -- 1 -- 2`, there's exactly one walk of length 2 from `0` to `2`, but two distinct walks of length 2 that start and end at `1` (bouncing off either neighbor and back): ::: {#d741707a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() g.add_node(label="0") g.add_node(label="1") g.add_node(label="2") g.add_edge("0", "1") g.add_edge("1", "2") walks = g.count_walks(2) node_0 = g.get_id_from_label("0") node_1 = g.get_id_from_label("1") node_2 = g.get_id_from_label("2") # Returns 1 (path: 0 -> 1 -> 2) walks[node_0][node_2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#36f734e4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns 2 (1 -> 0 -> 1 and 1 -> 2 -> 1) walks[node_1][node_1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: A triangle has cycles, so walks of length 3 can return to their starting node by going all the way around, or by bouncing back and forth on one edge: ::: {#ab259936 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() for i in range(3): g.add_node(label=str(i)) g.add_edge("0", "1") g.add_edge("1", "2") g.add_edge("2", "0") walks = g.count_walks(3) node_0 = g.get_id_from_label("0") # Returns 2 (0->1->2->0 and 0->1->0->0) walks[node_0][node_0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Summing over every entry in the result gives the total number of walks of that length anywhere in the graph: ::: {#03b31c5d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} total = sum(sum(targets.values()) for targets in walks.values()) # Total walks of length 3 in the triangle total ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 24 ``` ::: ::: Indexing by a single source node isolates just the walks that start there: ::: {#9249de11 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} source_walks = walks[node_0] # Returns the number of length-3 walks starting from node 0 sum(source_walks.values()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 8 ``` ::: :::
